notes.short: “You neatly set aside”: praise that rebukes
notes.about: Jesus seems to praise the Pharisees and scribes for how neatly they set aside God's command. He means the opposite: they had done evil. The next verses show how: their tradition kept a man from doing anything for his father or mother.

figure.name: Irony
figure.means: that they did evil, not well, in setting aside God's command for their tradition

original.note: In Mark's Greek “neatly” is kalōs, “well”, a word that means suitably or becomingly.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under irony spoken by God, brought out by the word for well, which means suitably: they did evil, not well. Clarke calls the word a strong irony: how noble their conduct, to annul God's commandments for their own traditions.
notes.limit: Not every writer reads irony here: some take the word plainly, as wholly, and others read the words as a question or as praise of their cunning.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Divine Irony, p. 811
cites.quote: Here the Irony is beautifully brought out by translating καλῶς (kalōs) “full well.” καλῶς means with propriety, suitably, becomingly. ... “Well do ye reject.” No, ye do evil!
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Full well - Καλως, - a strong irony. How noble is your conduct! From conscientious attachment to your own traditions ye have annihilated the commandments of God!
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “Fishers of men”: winning people for Christ
notes.about: Jesus finds two fishermen at their nets and says He will make them fishers of men. Their old work becomes a picture of the new: they will bring people to Christ through the gospel, as they once drew fish from the sea. Matthew 4:19 gives the same call.

figure.name: Hypocatastasis
figure.means: men who win others to Christ, gathering them in by the gospel

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Mark 1:17 under Hypocatastasis: the Lord neither says like fishers nor uses a direct metaphor, so the likeness is only implied. Henry says ministers are to fish for souls and win them to Christ, and Benson that they would draw men in by the net of the gospel. Calvin, on the same call in Luke 5:10, says Christ alluded to fishing when He spoke of preaching the gospel.
notes.limit: One writer calls the picture a metaphor. Either way, the fishermen's old work stands for their new work of winning people.

cites.quote: The Lord does not say like fishers, nor does He use direct metaphor. The resemblance is only by implication.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The business of ministers is to fish for souls, and win them to Christ. ... Ministers, in preaching the gospel, cast the net into the waters
I will enable you to draw them into my true church by the net of my gospel.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: As to the meaning of the metaphor, fishers of men, there is no necessity for a minute investigation. Yet, as it was drawn from the present occurrence, the allusion which Christ made to fishing, when he spoke of the preaching of the Gospel, was appropriate

notes.short: “Sabbath” and “man” come back in reverse order
notes.about: The saying names the Sabbath and man, then names them again in reverse order. Turning the words around sets the two in contrast: the Sabbath was made for man, and man was not made for the Sabbath.

figure.name: Antimetabole
figure.words: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath
figure.means: the Sabbath was made for man, not the other way round: man was not made for the Sabbath

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Antimetabole, or Counterchange, marking the words a b b a.
notes.limit: The note is about how the words are set out.

cites.quote: a “The sabbath b was made for man, b and not man for a the sabbath.”

notes.short: Truth at both ends, no favoritism in the middle
notes.about: The questioners call Jesus honest and say He teaches the way of God in accordance with the truth: these are the outer lines. In the two inner lines He seeks favor from no one and is impartial.

lines.words: we know that You are honest
and seek favor from no one.
and teach the way of God in accordance with the truth.

notes.evidence: Boys sets out the questioners' words in four lines: truth in the first and last, independence in the two between. He notes that in Matthew's account of the same words the clauses come in the order a reader would expect.

cites.quote: In a. and a., truth; in b. and b., independence. … In St. Matthew the clauses are placed in what, according to our notions of arrangement, we should call their natural order. But God's ways are not always our ways.
